title: David Dhawan Has Directed His Last Film. Varun Is Trying to Send Him Off With a Hit.
excerpt: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai opened at ₹8.65 crore but flatlined on Day 2. It is a love letter from a son to his father — and a test of whether Bollywood still has room for the rom-com.
body:
There is something unbearably poignant about watching a filmmaker say goodbye. **David Dhawan** — the man who gave us *Coolie No. 1*, *Judwaa*, *Biwi No. 1*, and roughly half the comedies that soundtracked every NRI living room through the '90s and 2000s — has directed his 46th and final film. **Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai** released on June 6, and it is, by every metric, a farewell.

The setup is quintessential Dhawan: **Varun Dhawan** plays the charming idiot, **Mrunal Thakur** is the girl he doesn't deserve, and **Pooja Hegde** is the complication. Throw in **Maniesh Paul**, **Mouni Roy**, **Chunky Pandey**, **Jonny Lever**, and **Rajpal Yadav**, and you have the kind of ensemble that could only exist in a David Dhawan film — loud, chaotic, deeply uncool, and somehow irresistible.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DZMfuByjLyh/

> "Now you can't stop anyone. Every producer is of the opinion that 'Main kyun aage jaau?'" — Trade veteran Taran Adarsh on June's crowded release calendar

The opening day brought in **₹8.65 crore net** domestically, with an overseas gross of **₹2.5 crore**, pushing the worldwide Day 1 total to **₹12.70 crore**. For context, that's the biggest romantic opening of 2026 in Bollywood — nearly double what *Pati Patni Aur Woh Do* managed. But by Day 2, the momentum stalled. Saturday added just **₹7.50 crore**, a flat hold that has the trade projecting a first weekend of **₹23-25 crore**.

The numbers are adequate, not electric. And they tell a bigger story.

Bollywood's mid-range rom-com is fighting for its life. The culprit, as every trade analyst will tell you over chai, is the 8-week OTT window. Why spend ₹500 at PVR when you can wait two months and watch it on your couch? *Sunny Sanskari Ki Tulsi Kumari*, Varun's last rom-com, ended its run at around **₹60 crore**. *Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai* is tracking on similar lines — respectable, but a far cry from the ₹100-crore clubs that David Dhawan routinely minted a decade ago.

But here's what the numbers don't capture: the sheer warmth of the thing. Reviews have been mixed-to-positive, with most critics noting that Dhawan père has made exactly the film he wanted to make — a big, broad, unapologetically old-school entertainer. Varun, for his part, is clearly performing with something beyond commercial ambition. This is a son making sure his father's last day on set ends with the audience clapping.

The supporting cast does heavy lifting. **Jonny Lever** reportedly has a 15-minute stretch in the second half that's being called his best work in years. **Rajpal Yadav** gets the physical comedy showcase. And **Mrunal Thakur**, increasingly Bollywood's most reliable leading lady, anchors the emotional core with a performance that's smarter than the script probably deserves.

For the diaspora, the film hits a particular nerve. David Dhawan's movies are woven into the fabric of NRI weekends — the rented VHS tapes, the Sunday afternoon family screenings, the Govinda impressions at Diwali parties. This is the end of that lineage. Whether you love the genre or merely tolerate it, there's no denying its cultural weight.

The ticket strategy also deserves a mention. The makers offered **50% off** on opening day tickets — a move that boosted footfall but also revealed how price-sensitive the audience has become for anything that isn't a tentpole franchise. It worked: family audiences in mass centres showed up in droves for evening and night shows, with occupancy climbing from 9% in mornings to over 30% at night. Delhi NCR, Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad led the charge.

**Where to watch:** *Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai* is currently in theatres across India, the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and the Middle East. The OTT window is expected in approximately 8 weeks.

The question isn't really whether this film will be a blockbuster. David Dhawan has made enough of those. The question is whether this goodbye — funny, messy, sentimental, a little too loud — feels right. For anyone who grew up on his films, the answer is yes. Even if you're crying into your popcorn.
